# Boolean, Free, and Classical Cumulants as Tree Enumerations

**Authors:** Colin Defant Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: colindefant@gmail.com and Mitchell Lee Address: Department of Mathematics, Harvard University, Cambridge, MA 02138, USA Email address: mitchell@math.harvard.edu

## Abstract

Defant found that the relationship between a sequence of (univariate) classical cumulants and the corresponding sequence of (univariate) free cumulants can be described combinatorially in terms of families of binary plane trees called troupes. Using a generalization of troupes that we call weighted troupes, we generalize this result to allow for multivariate cumulants. Our result also gives a combinatorial description of the corresponding Boolean cumulants. This allows us to answer a question of Defant regarding his troupe transform. We also provide explicit distributions whose cumulants correspond to some specific weighted troupes.

## 1. Introduction

Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a unital associative algebra over a commutative ring $\mathbb{K}$ , and let $\varphi\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{K}$ be a unital linear functional. The pair $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ is called a noncommutative probability space (over $\mathbb{K}$ ), and the functional $\varphi$ is called a noncommutative expectation. Let $(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ be a tuple of elements of $\mathcal{A}$ . We associate to this tuple three important quantities: the classical cumulant $K_{n}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , the free cumulant $R_{n}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ , and the Boolean cumulant $B_{n}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ . The classical cumulant $K_{n}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is informally a measure of the dependence of $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ , whereas the free cumulant $R_{n}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})$ is an analogue used in the free probability theory of Voiculescu [MS17, Voi85, Voi91, Voi94, VDN92]. Classical, free, and Boolean cumulants are all related by formulas involving sums over particular sets of partitions of the set $[n]:=\{1,\ldots,n\}$ [AHLV15].

If the variables $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}$ are all equal, then more is known. In 2013, Josuat-Vergès found a combinatorial expansion of the negative classical cumulant $-K_{n}(X,\ldots,X)$ into negative free cumulants $-R_{i}(X,\ldots,X)$ for $i\leq n$ [JV13]. In 2022, Defant proved that the coefficients of Josuat-Vergès’s expansion count objects called valid hook configurations, which also appear in the study of West’s stack-sorting map [Def22]. This connection allowed Defant to prove several results about the stack-sorting map.

Defant also found that the relationship between free and classical cumulants is encoded by special families of binary plane trees called troupes. Our main theorem (Theorem 4.1) generalizes this result in three ways. First, our theorem deals with a new generalization of troupes that we call weighted troupes. Second, our theorem does not require the elements $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\in\mathcal{A}$ to be all equal. Third, our theorem handles Boolean cumulants in addition to classical and free cumulants.

A troupe is a family of binary plane trees satisfying certain conditions related to an operation called insertion. A branch is a binary plane tree in which no vertex has more than one child. In [Def22], Defant proved that each troupe is uniquely determined by the set of branches that it contains and that every set of branches generates a unique troupe. He then defined the troupe transform to be the transform that takes as input a sequence $(\omega_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ enumerating a set of branches and outputs the sequence $(\widecheck{\omega}_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ enumerating the troupe generated by that set of branches. He asked what could be said about the relationship between the generating functions

$$ \mathscr{B}(x)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\omega_{n}x^{n}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathscr{T}(x)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\widecheck{\omega}_{n}x^{n} $$

([Def22, Question 9.1]). In particular, he asked what conditions on $\mathscr{B}(x)$ would guarantee that $\mathscr{T}(x)$ is algebraic. Using Theorem 4.1, we completely resolve these questions. Namely, we show in Theorem 5.1 that

$$ \mathscr{T}(x)=\mathscr{B}\left(\frac{x}{1-x\mathscr{T}(x)}\right); $$

this implies (see Corollary 5.2) that $\mathscr{T}(x)$ is algebraic if and only if $\mathscr{B}(x)$ is algebraic. (In fact, our Theorem 5.1 is more general because it deals with weighted troupes instead of ordinary troupes.)

Section 2 provides preliminaries concerning partitions, cumulants, and binary plane trees. In Section 3, we define and provide examples of weighted troupes, and we discuss some of their properties. In particular, we show how a binary plane tree can be decomposed into branches called its insertion factors. In Section 4, we state and prove our main theorem (Theorem 4.1) regarding weighted troupes and cumulants. In Section 5, we prove Theorem 5.1, which completely describes the troupe transform. Section 6 is devoted to explaining how one can easily compute the insertion factors of a decreasing binary plane tree directly from the permutation corresponding to it via the inorder bijection. Finally, in Section 7, we compute explicit distributions whose cumulants correspond to some especially notable weighted troupes.

## 2. Background

### 2.1. Partitions

Let $Y$ be a finite set. A partition of $Y$ is a collection of nonempty disjoint sets, called blocks, whose union is $Y$ . For any partition $\pi$ of $Y$ , we define an equivalence relation $\sim_{\pi}$ on $Y$ , where $i\sim_{\pi}j$ if and only if $i$ and $j$ are in the same block of $\pi$ . In this way, partitions of $Y$ are in bijective correspondence with equivalence relations on $Y$ .

Suppose that $Y$ is totally ordered. We say that a partition $\pi$ of $Y$ is an interval partition if there do not exist $i,j,k\in Y$ with $i<j<k$ such that $i\sim_{\pi}k\not\sim_{\pi}j$ . We say that $\pi$ is noncrossing if there do not exist $i,j,k,\ell\in Y$ with $i<j<k<\ell$ such that $i\sim_{\pi}k$ , $j\sim_{\pi}\ell$ , and $i\not\sim_{\pi}j$ . We say that a noncrossing partition $\pi$ of $Y$ is irreducible if $\min Y\sim_{\pi}\max Y$ . We write $\Pi(n)$ , $\mathrm{Int}(n)$ , $\mathrm{NC}(n)$ , and $\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}(n)$ for the set of partitions of $[n]$ , the set of interval partitions of $[n]$ , the set of noncrossing partitions of $[n]$ , and the set of irreducible noncrossing partitions of $[n]$ , respectively.

Let $\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ denote the symmetric group whose elements are permutations of $[n]$ . The descent set of a permutation ${\sigma=\sigma(1)\cdots\sigma(n)\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}}$ is $\mathrm{Des}(w)=\{i\in[n-1]:\sigma(i)>\sigma(i+1)\}$ . Let ${\mathrm{des}(\sigma)=|\mathrm{Des}(\sigma)|}$ . The descending runs of $\sigma$ are the maximal consecutive decreasing subsequences of $\sigma$ ; note that $\sigma$ has $n-\mathrm{des}(\sigma)$ descending runs. Let $\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ be the partition

$$ \{D_{1}(\sigma),\ldots,D_{n-\mathrm{des}(\sigma)}(\sigma)\}\in\Pi(n), $$

where $D_{j}(\sigma)$ is the set of numbers appearing in the $j$ th descending run of $\sigma$ . For example,

$$ \mathrm{druns}(854791632)=\{\{4,5,8\},\{7\},\{1,9\},\{2,3,6\}\}\in\Pi(9). $$

### 2.2. Cumulants

Let $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ be a noncommutative probability space over a commutative ring $\mathbb{K}$ . For $n\geq 1$ , there are three multilinear functionals $K_{n},R_{n},B_{n}\colon\mathcal{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{K}$ , called the classical cumulant, free cumulant, and Boolean cumulant, respectively.

For any set $U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\}\subseteq[n]$ with $u_{1}<\cdots<u_{k}$ and any $X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}\in\mathcal{A}$ , define $K_{U}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=K_{k}(X_{u_{1}},\ldots,X_{u_{k}})$ , and similarly define $R_{U}$ and $B_{U}$ . For $\pi\in\Pi(n)$ , define

$$ K_{\pi}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=\prod_{U\in\pi}K_{U}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}), $$

and similarly define $R_{\pi}$ and $B_{\pi}$ .

The functions $K_{n},R_{n},B_{n}\colon\mathcal{A}^{n}\to\mathbb{K}$ are uniquely determined by the following equations [AHLV15, Theorem 2.5]:

$$ \displaystyle\varphi(X_{1}\cdots X_{n}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\Pi(n)}K_{\pi}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}), \displaystyle\varphi(X_{1}\cdots X_{n}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{NC}(n)}R_{\pi}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}), \displaystyle\varphi(X_{1}\cdots X_{n}) \displaystyle=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{Int}_{n}}B_{\pi}(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}). $$

Let $X\in\mathcal{A}$ . For $n\geq 0$ , the $n$ th moment of $X$ is $\varphi(X^{n})$ . The moment-generating function of $X$ is

$$ M_{X}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\varphi(X^{n})\frac{t^{n}}{n!}, $$

the exponential generating function of the moments of $X$ . This is well defined as long as $\mathbb{K}$ contains $\mathbb{Q}$ . The classical cumulants $K_{n}(X,\ldots,X)$ can be computed from $M_{X}(t)$ via the equation

$$ \sum_{n\geq 1}K_{n}(X,\ldots,X)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}=\log M_{X}(t). $$

### 2.3. Binary Plane Trees

A binary plane tree is a rooted tree $T$ in which each child of a vertex is designated as a left child or a right child and no vertex can have more than one left child or more than one right child. The empty binary plane tree is denoted $\varnothing$ . When there is no risk of confusion, we also use the symbol $T$ to denote the set of vertices of the tree $T$ . The size of $T$ , denoted $|T|$ , is the number of vertices in $T$ . Let $\mathsf{BPT}$ denote the set of all binary plane trees (up to isomorphism), and let $\mathsf{BPT}_{n}$ denote the set of all binary plane trees of size $n$ . It is a classical result that $|\mathsf{BPT}_{n}|=C_{n}$ , where $C_{n}=\frac{1}{n+1}\binom{2n}{n}$ denotes the $n$ th Catalan number.

The inorder on a binary plane tree $T$ is the unique total order on the vertices of $T$ such that for each vertex $v$ of $T$ , all the vertices in the left subtree of $v$ precede $v$ , which in turn precedes all the vertices in the right subtree of $v$ . The postorder on a binary plane tree $T$ is the unique total order on the vertices of $T$ such that for each vertex $v$ of $T$ , all the vertices in the left subtree of $v$ precede all the vertices in the right subtree of $v$ , which in turn precede $v$ .

A labeling of a binary plane tree $T$ is a function $\mathcal{L}\colon T\to\mathbb{N}$ . The label of a vertex $v$ under a labeling $\mathcal{L}$ is the integer $\mathcal{L}(v)$ . We say that a labeling of $T$ is standard if it uses each of the labels $1,\ldots,|T|$ exactly once. A labeling of a binary plane tree is decreasing if the label of each vertex is greater than the labels of its children.

Given a binary plane tree $T$ , we will now describe two important standard labelings of $T$ . The inorder labeling of $T$ , denoted $\mathcal{I}_{T}$ , assigns the vertices of $T$ the labels $1,\ldots,n$ in inorder. The postorder labeling of $T$ , denoted $\mathcal{P}_{T}$ , assigns the vertices of $T$ the labels $1,\ldots,n$ in postorder. Note that the postorder labeling of $T$ is decreasing. See Figure 1.

Let $\mathsf{DBPT}$ denote the set of all trees $T\in\mathsf{BPT}$ that are equipped with a standard decreasing labeling $\mathcal{L}$ . Formally, $\mathsf{DBPT}$ is the set of all pairs $(T,\mathcal{L})$ , where $T\in\mathsf{BPT}$ and $\mathcal{L}$ is a standard decreasing labeling of $T$ . However, we will usually refer to an element of $\mathsf{DBPT}$ using just the letter $T$ and leave the labeling $\mathcal{L}$ implicit. We call the elements of $\mathsf{DBPT}$ decreasing binary plane trees. Let $\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}$ denote the set of all decreasing binary plane trees of size $n$ . There is an injection $\iota\colon\mathsf{BPT}\to\mathsf{DBPT}$ that equips each binary plane tree $T$ with its postorder labeling.

A branch is a nonempty binary plane tree in which every vertex has at most one child. Let $\mathsf{Branch}$ denote the set of all branches, and let $\mathsf{Branch}_{n}$ denote the set of all branches of size $n$ . Clearly, we have $|\mathsf{Branch}_{n}|=2^{n-1}$ for $n\geq 1$ .

*Figure 1. The inorder labeling (left) and postorder labeling (right) of a binary plane tree.*

We now define functions $\alpha,\beta\colon\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ . Given $(T,\mathcal{L})\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}$ and a label $k\in[n]$ , let

$$ \alpha(T,\mathcal{L})(k)=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{I}_{T}^{-1}(k))\quad\text{and}\quad\beta(T,\mathcal{L})(k)=\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{P}_{T}^{-1}(k)). $$

In other words, $\alpha(T)$ is the permutation formed by reading the labels of the vertices of $T$ in inorder, while $\beta(T)$ is the permutation formed by reading the labels of the vertices of $T$ in postorder.

It is well known that $\alpha$ is a bijection. West’s stack-sorting map is the function $s\colon\mathfrak{S}_{n}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ given by

$$ s(\sigma)=\beta(\alpha^{-1}(\sigma)). $$

Fix an index set $I$ (possibly infinite). An $I$ -coloring of a binary plane tree $T$ is a function $\chi\colon T\sqcup\{\boxminus\}\to I$ , where $\boxminus$ is a special symbol that denotes an element not in $T$ . Let $\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ denote the set of all $I$ -colored binary plane trees, let $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ denote the set of all $I$ -colored branches, and let $\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ denote the set of all $I$ -colored binary plane trees equipped with a decreasing labeling. We have an injection $\iota\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ that assigns each $I$ -colored binary plane tree the postorder labeling.

Much of the flavor of our results is retained if $I=\{\star\}$ is a singleton, so the reader may find it helpful to keep that special case in mind. In that case, $\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ , $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ , and $\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ are in obvious bijection with $\mathsf{BPT}$ , $\mathsf{Branch}$ , and $\mathsf{DBPT}$ , respectively. When there is no risk of confusion, we will sometimes use the notations $\mathsf{BPT}$ , $\mathsf{Branch}$ , and $\mathsf{DBPT}$ as shorthand for $\mathsf{BPT}(\{\star\})$ , $\mathsf{Branch}(\{\star\})$ , and $\mathsf{DBPT}(\{\star\})$ , respectively.

Given $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ , define $\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ to be the set of all $T\in\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ such that $\chi(\boxminus)=i_{n}$ and such that $\chi(v)=i_{\mathcal{L}(v)}$ for all $v\in T$ .

Define $\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})=\iota^{-1}(\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}))$ . This is the set of all $I$ -colored binary plane trees such that the colors of the vertices form the sequence $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n-1}$ when read in postorder and such that the color of $\boxminus$ is $i_{n}$ .

Define $\mathsf{Branch}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})=\mathsf{Branch}(I)\cap\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ .

Given a tree $T\in\mathsf{DBPT}$ and a vertex $v\in\mathsf{DBPT}$ with exactly one child, we can swing $T$ at $v$ by changing the subtree of $v$ from a left subtree to a right subtree or vice versa. In a similar way, we may swing trees in $\mathsf{BPT}$ , $\mathsf{Branch}$ , $\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ , $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ , $\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ , $\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ , $\mathsf{Branch}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ , and $\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ .

## 3. Insertion and Troupes

Let $T_{1},T_{2}\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ , and let $v$ be a vertex of $T_{1}$ . We will now define a new $I$ -colored tree $\nabla_{v}(T_{1},T_{2})\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ , called the insertion of $T_{2}$ into $T_{1}$ at $v$ . First, form a new tree $T_{1}^{v}$ from $T_{1}$ by extending $v$ into a left edge; identify $v$ with the bottom vertex of this left edge, and call the upper vertex $v^{*}$ . Next, attach $T_{2}$ as the right subtree of $v^{*}$ . To define the $I$ -coloring $\chi$ of $\nabla_{v}(T_{1},T_{2})$ , let $\chi_{1}$ and $\chi_{2}$ be the $I$ -colorings of $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ , respectively. For $u\in T_{1}\sqcup\{\boxminus\}$ , let $\chi(u)=\chi_{1}$ . For $u^{\prime}\in T_{2}$ , let $\chi(u^{\prime})=\chi_{2}(u^{\prime})$ . Finally, let $\chi(v^{*})=\chi_{2}(\boxminus)$ .

#### Example 3.1.

Let $I$ be a $3$ -element set whose elements are represented by the colors cyan, yellow, and magenta. Consider the $I$ -colored binary plane trees $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ shown on the left of Figure 2, where the color of $\boxminus$ in each $I$ -colored tree is represented by a colored version of the symbol $\boxminus$ floating above and to the left of the root of the tree. Let $v\in T_{1}$ be as indicated. Then the insertion of $T_{2}$ into $T_{1}$ at $v$ is the $I$ -colored binary plane tree shown on the right of Figure 2.

*Figure 2. Two $I$ -colored binary planes trees $T_{1}$ and $T_{2}$ (left) and the insertion of $T_{2}$ into $T_{1}$ at the vertex $v$ (right).*

Every tree $T\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ can be formed from branches by repeatedly performing the insertion operation. We now describe how this is done. Let $\Lambda_{T}$ be the set consisting of $\boxminus$ and the vertices of $T$ with two children. Define the function $\gamma\colon T\cup\{\boxminus\}\to\Lambda_{T}$ as follows. If $u\in\Lambda_{T}$ , then let $\gamma(u)=u$ . If $u\not\in\Lambda_{T}$ and there is a vertex $v\in\Lambda_{T}\setminus\{\boxminus\}$ such that the right subtree of $v$ contains $u$ , then let $\gamma(u)$ be the lowest such vertex $v$ . Otherwise, let $\gamma(u)=\boxminus$ . Define $\pi_{T}=\{\gamma^{-1}(v):v\in\Lambda_{T}\}$ ; this is a partition of $T\cup\{\boxminus\}$ .

Let $v\in\Lambda_{T}$ . Define a binary plane tree $T_{v}\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ on the vertex set $\gamma^{-1}(v)\setminus\{v\}$ as follows. For any $u,w\in\gamma^{-1}(v)\setminus\{v\}$ , we have that $w$ is a left (respectively, right) child of $u$ in $T_{v}$ if and only if $w$ appears in the left (respectively, right) subtree of $u$ in $T$ and there is no element of $\gamma^{-1}(v)$ between $w$ and $u$ in $T$ . Clearly, $T_{v}$ is a branch. The $I$ -coloring of $T_{v}$ is defined as follows. For $u\in\gamma^{-1}(v)\setminus\{v\}$ , the color of $u$ in $T_{v}$ is the same as its color in $T$ . The color of $\boxminus$ in $T_{v}$ is the color of $v$ in $T$ . We call the trees $T_{v}\in\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ for $v\in\Lambda_{T}$ the insertion factors of $T$ .

#### Example 3.2.

Let $T$ be the $I$ -colored binary plane tree shown on the top of Figure 3. We have $\Lambda_{T}=\{r_{4},r_{8},r_{9},\boxminus\}$ , so $\pi_{T}=\{\gamma^{-1}(r_{4}),\gamma^{-1}(r_{8}),\gamma^{-1}(r_{9}),\gamma^{-1}(\boxminus)\}$ , where

$$ \gamma^{-1}(r_{4})=\{r_{2},r_{3},r_{4}\},\quad\gamma^{-1}(r_{8})=\{r_{6},r_{7},r_{8}\},\quad\gamma^{-1}(r_{9})=\{r_{5},r_{9}\},\quad\gamma^{-1}(\boxminus)=\{r_{1},\boxminus\}. $$

The insertion factors of $T$ are $T_{r_{4}}$ , $T_{r_{8}}$ , $T_{r_{9}}$ , and $T_{\boxminus}$ , which are shown on the bottom of Figure 3.

*Figure 3. An $I$ -colored binary plane tree (top) and its insertion factors (bottom).*

Note that multiple insertion factors of $T$ may be isomorphic to each other. (In Example 3.2, $T_{r_{9}}$ and $T_{\boxminus}$ are isomorphic.) The collection of insertion factors of $T$ , up to isomorphism, is a multiset $\mathsf{IF}(T)\subseteq\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ . The following proposition is immediate from the definitions.

#### Proposition 3.3.

Let $T_{1},T_{2}\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ , and let $v$ be a vertex of $T_{1}$ . Then $\mathsf{IF}(\nabla_{v}(T_{1},T_{2}))$ is the multiset union of $\mathsf{IF}(T_{1})$ and $\mathsf{IF}(T_{2})$ .

Proposition 3.3 implies that every tree can be formed from its insertion factors by repeatedly performing the insertion operation.

#### Remark 3.4.

Let us make an analogy between binary plane trees and classical algebraic structures (such as modules over a ring). One should view $I$ -colored branches as the “indecomposable” objects of $\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ . Each tree $T\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ can be obtained from a sequence of $I$ -colored branches via iterated insertions. Such a sequence of $I$ -colored branches is not necessarily unique. However, Proposition 3.3 implies that the multiset of $I$ -colored branches appearing in the sequence is uniquely determined by $T$ (it is $\mathsf{IF}(T)$ ). Thus, one can view Proposition 3.3 as an analogue of the Jordan–Hölder theorem for binary plane trees.

A troupe is a subset $\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ such that for all $T_{1},T_{2}\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ and all vertices $v\in T_{1}$ , we have $\nabla_{v}(T_{1},T_{2})\in\mathbf{T}$ if and only if $T_{1}\in\mathbf{T}$ and $T_{2}\in\mathbf{T}$ . Troupes were introduced in [Def22]; we generalize them as follows. Let $\mathbb{K}$ be a commutative ring. A weighted troupe is a function $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{K}$ with the following properties:

- • $\bm{\tau}(\varnothing)=0$ ;

- • For all $T_{1},T_{2}\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ and all vertices $v\in T_{1}$ , we have $\bm{\tau}(\nabla_{v}(T_{1},T_{2}))=\bm{\tau}(T_{1})\bm{\tau}(T_{2})$ .

Observe that the indicator function of a troupe is a weighted troupe.

Let $\bm{\tau}|_{\mathsf{Branch}(I)}$ denote the restriction of a weighted troupe $\bm{\tau}$ to $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ . The following result is a generalization of [Def22, Theorem 2.3] to weighted troupes.

#### Proposition 3.5.

The map $\bm{\tau}\mapsto\bm{\tau}|_{\mathsf{Branch}(I)}$ is a bijection from the set of weighted troupes to the set of functions from $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ to $\mathbb{K}$ .

#### Proof.

Let $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{K}$ be a function. By Proposition 3.3, we have that $\bm{\tau}$ is a weighted troupe if and only if $\bm{\tau}(\varnothing)=0$ and

$$ \bm{\tau}(T)=\prod_{T^{\prime}\in\mathsf{IF}(T)}\bm{\tau}(T^{\prime}) $$

for all $T\in\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ . The proposition follows. ∎

For $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{K}$ and $T\in\mathsf{DBPT}(I)$ , we will, slightly abusing notation, write $\bm{\tau}(T)$ to denote the result of applying $\bm{\tau}$ to the underlying (unlabeled) tree of $T$ .

Let us briefly mention some examples of troupes and weighted troupes. We will revisit some of these examples in Section 7.

- (1) The simplest example of a troupe is $\mathsf{BPT}(I)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ ; its set of branches is the entire set $\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ .

- (2) A nonempty binary plane tree is called full if no vertex has exactly one child. The set of full $I$ -colored binary plane trees is a troupe; its set of branches is $\mathsf{Branch}_{1}(I)$ .

- (3) A Motzkin tree is a nonempty binary plane tree in which every vertex that has a right child also has a left child. The set of $I$ -colored Moztkin trees is a troupe; its set of branches is precisely the set of nonempty $I$ -colored branches with no right edges.

- (4) Fix a subset $J\subseteq I$ . Let ${\bf T}$ be the set of nonempty $I$ -colored binary plane trees such that every vertex with a left child is assigned a color from $J$ and $\boxminus$ is also assigned a color from $J$ . Then ${\bf T}$ is a troupe.

- (5) Let $t_{1}$ and $t_{2}$ be indeterminates. Let $\mathrm{right}(T)$ and $\mathrm{two}(T)$ denote the number of right edges and the number of vertices with two children, respectively, in a binary plane tree $T$ . If ${\bf T}$ is a troupe, then the map $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{C}[t_{1},t_{2}]$ defined by

$$ \bm{\tau}(T)=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathbf{T}}(T)t_{1}^{\mathrm{right}(T)+1}t_{2}^{\mathrm{two}(T)+1} $$

is a weighted troupe.

- (6) Let $t$ be an indeterminate, and let $J\subseteq I$ . Let $\mathbf{T}$ be a troupe, and define $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{C}[t]$ by

$$ \bm{\tau}(T)=\mathbbm{1}_{\mathbf{T}}(T)t^{|\chi^{-1}(J)|}, $$

where $\chi$ is the $I$ -coloring of $T$ . Then $\bm{\tau}$ is a weighted troupe.

## 4. Boolean, Free, and Classical Cumulants as Tree Enumerations

The following theorem generalizes [Def22, Theorem 6.1] in three ways. First, it deals with weighted troupes rather than (ordinary) troupes. Second, it involves potentially mixed cumulants rather than only cumulants of a single variable. Third, it includes a condition about Boolean cumulants in addition to the conditions about classical and free cumulants. If $I=\{\star\}$ is a singleton, then we recover [Def22, Theorem 6.1] from parts (i) and (ii) in the following theorem. We encourage the reader to refer to Examples 4.2 and 4.3 while reading the following proof.

#### Theorem 4.1.

Let $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ be a noncommutative probability space over a commutative ring $\mathbb{K}$ . Let $I$ be an index set, and let $(X_{i})_{i\in I}$ be a sequence of elements of $\mathcal{A}$ indexed by the set $I$ . Let $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}(I)\to\mathbb{K}$ be a weighted troupe. The following are equivalent:

- (i) For all $n\geq 1$ and all $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ , we have

$$ -K_{n}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

- (ii) For all $n\geq 1$ and all $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ , we have

$$ -R_{n}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

- (iii) For all $n\geq 1$ and all $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ , we have

$$ -B_{n}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

#### Proof.

For any subset $U=\{u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\}\subseteq[n]$ with $u_{1}<\cdots<u_{k}$ , let $i_{U}=(i_{u_{1}},\ldots,i_{u_{k}})$ .

By (1), (2), and (3), we have $K_{1}(X)=R_{1}(X)=B_{1}(X)=\varphi(X)$ for all $X\in\mathcal{A}$ . Therefore (since $\bm{\tau}(\varnothing)=0$ ), each of (i), (ii), and (iii) implies that ${K_{1}(X_{i})=R_{1}(X_{i})=B_{1}(X_{i})=\varphi(X_{i})=0}$ for all $i\in I$ . Hence, we may assume in what follows that $K_{1}(X_{i})=R_{1}(X_{i})=B_{1}(X_{i})=\varphi(X_{i})=0$ for all $i\in I$ .

First, we will show that (ii) is equivalent to (iii). Fix $n\geq 1$ and $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ . By [AHLV15, Equation 1.4], we have that

$$ -R_{n}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}(n)}\prod_{U\in\pi}(-B_{U}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})). $$

Therefore, it suffices to show that

$$ \sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\bm{\tau}(T)=\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}(n)}\prod_{U\in\pi}\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{U})}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

Let $\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}^{\geq 2}(n)$ be the set of all irreducible noncrossing partitions of $[n]$ whose blocks all have cardinality at least $2$ . Observe that the outer summand on the right-hand side of (6) vanishes for $\pi\not\in\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}^{\geq 2}(n)$ . Let $P(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ be the set of pairs $(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ with $\pi\in\mathrm{NC}_{\text{irr}}^{\geq 2}(n)$ and $T_{U}\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{U})$ for all $U\in\pi$ . The right-hand side of (6) can be expanded to

$$ \sum_{(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})\in P(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\prod_{U\in\pi}\bm{\tau}(T_{U}). $$

Therefore, to prove (6), it suffices to exhibit a bijection $\Psi\colon P(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})\to\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ such that if $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})=T$ , then the multiset of branches $T_{U}$ for $U\in\pi$ is $\mathsf{IF}(T)$ .

Let $(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})\in P(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . For each $U\in\pi$ , we may assume that the vertex set of the branch $T_{U}$ is $U\setminus\max U$ and that each non-root vertex of $T_{U}$ is smaller than its parent. The binary plane tree $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})\in\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ can be constructed as follows.

- • The vertices of $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ are the integers $1,\ldots,n-1$ .

- • Let $j\in[n-1]$ , and let $U\in\pi$ be the block containing $j$ . – If $j=\min U$ , then $j$ is a leaf of $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ . – If $\min U<j<\max U$ , then $j-1$ is the unique child of $j$ in $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ ; moreover, $j-1$ is a left (respectively, right) child of $j$ in $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ if and only if $j$ has a left (respectively, right) child in $T_{U}$ . – If $j=\max U$ , then $j$ has two children in $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ ; the right child of $j$ is $j-1$ , and the left child of $j$ is $\min U-1$ .

- • The $I$ -coloring is given by $\chi(j)=i_{j}$ for $j\in[n-1]$ and $\chi(\boxminus)=i_{n}$ .

We need to check that $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ is actually a binary plane tree whose postorder agrees with the usual total order on $[n]$ . To do so, we describe a recursive procedure for constructing $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ . Let $U_{1},\ldots,U_{r}$ be the blocks of $\pi$ , listed so that $\min U_{1}<\cdots<\min U_{r}$ . For $2\leq i\leq r$ , let $v_{i}=\min U_{i}-1$ . Let $\Upsilon_{1}=T_{U_{1}}$ . For $2\leq i\leq r$ , let $\Upsilon_{i}=\nabla_{v_{i}}(\Upsilon_{i-1},T_{U_{i}})$ , and rename the new vertex $v_{i}^{*}$ created during this insertion as $\max U_{i}$ (so $\max U_{i}$ is the parent of $\min U_{i}-1$ in $\Upsilon_{i}$ ). It is straightforward to check that $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})=\Upsilon_{r}$ . The fact that $\Upsilon_{r}$ is a binary plane tree whose postorder agrees with the usual total order on $[n]$ follows from the definition of insertion and the fact that $\pi$ is an irreducible noncrossing partition.

Inversely, let $T\in\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . We will now describe $\Psi^{-1}(T)\in P(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . Using the notation from Section 3, we have that $\pi_{T}=\{\gamma^{-1}(v):v\in\Lambda_{T}\}$ is a partition of $T\cup\{\boxminus\}$ . Moreover, the blocks of $\pi_{T}$ correspond to the insertion factors of $T$ . By mapping $T$ to $[n-1]$ using the postorder labeling and mapping $\boxminus$ to $n$ , we may transport $\pi_{T}$ to a partition $\pi\in\Pi(n)$ . Again, each part $U\in\pi$ has a corresponding insertion factor $T_{U}\in\mathsf{Branch}(I)$ . Let $\Psi^{-1}(T)=(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})$ . The fact that $\pi$ is noncrossing is immediate from the definition of the postorder and the definition of $\gamma$ . Because each insertion factor contains at least one vertex together with the symbol $\boxminus$ , every block of $\pi$ has cardinality at least $2$ . To see that $\pi$ is irreducible, note that if $v$ is the first vertex in the postorder of $T$ , then $v$ cannot be in the right subtree of a vertex with two children, so $v$ and $\boxminus$ are both in $\gamma^{-1}(\boxminus)$ .

The functions $\Psi$ and $\Psi^{-1}$ described above are inverses. Therefore, $\Psi$ is a bijection. It follows directly from the definition of $\Psi^{-1}$ that if $\Psi(\pi,(T_{U})_{U\in\pi})=T$ , then the multiset of branches $T_{U}$ for $U\in\pi$ is $\mathsf{IF}(T)$ . This proves (6), so (ii) is equivalent to (iii).

Finally, we will show that (i) is equivalent to (iii). Once again, fix $n\geq 1$ and $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ . By [AHLV15, Corollary 1.6], we have

$$ -K_{n}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\sigma(1)=n\end{subarray}}\prod_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)}(-B_{U}(X_{i_{1}},\ldots,X_{i_{n}})). $$

Therefore, it suffices to show that

$$ \sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\bm{\tau}(T)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}\\
\sigma(1)=n\end{subarray}}\prod_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)}\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{U})}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

Let $\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ be the set of $\sigma\in\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ with $\sigma(1)=n$ such that all the blocks of $\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ have cardinality at least $2$ . Observe that the outer summand on the right-hand side of (8) vanishes for $\sigma\not\in\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ . Let $Q(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ be the set of pairs $(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ with $\sigma\in\mathfrak{D}_{n}$ and $T_{U}\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{U})$ for all $U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ . The right-hand side of (8) can be expanded to

$$ \sum_{(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})\in Q(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}\,\prod_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)}\bm{\tau}(T_{U}). $$

Therefore, to prove (8), it suffices to exhibit a bijection $\Phi\colon Q(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})\to\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ such that if $\Phi(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})=T$ , then the multiset of branches $T_{U}$ for $U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ is $\mathsf{IF}(T)$ .

Let $(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})\in Q(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . For each $U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ , we may assume that the vertex set of the branch $T_{U}$ is $U\setminus\max U$ and that each non-root vertex of $T_{U}$ is smaller than its parent. The decreasing binary plane tree $\Phi(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ can be constructed as follows. First, let $\sigma^{\star}\in\mathfrak{S}_{n-1}$ be the permutation formed by deleting the entry $n$ (i.e., the first entry) from $\sigma$ . Recall the bijection $\alpha\colon\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}\to\mathfrak{S}_{n-1}$ from Section 2.3. Let $\alpha^{-1}(\sigma^{*})=(T,\mathcal{L})$ . We may form a decreasing binary plane tree ${\tilde{\Phi}(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})\in\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})}$ from $(T,\mathcal{L})$ by defining a coloring $\chi$ of $T$ such that $\chi(\boxminus)=i_{n}$ and such that $\chi(v)=i_{\mathcal{L}(v)}$ for all $v\in T$ . Because $\sigma$ has no descending runs of length $1$ , the tree $\tilde{\Phi}(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ is a reverse Motzkin tree; that is, every vertex with a left child also has a right child. We will form $\Phi(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ by modifying $\tilde{\Phi}(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ as follows. Note that the non-leaf vertices of the branches $(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)}$ correspond to the vertices of $\tilde{\Phi}(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ with exactly one child. For each vertex of one of the branches $(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)}$ that has a left child, swing $\tilde{\Phi}(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ at the corresponding vertex. Let $\Phi(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ be the result of performing all these swings.

Inversely, let $T\in\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . We will now describe $\Phi^{-1}(T)\in Q(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ . First, let $\tilde{T}$ be the tree formed by swinging $T$ at each vertex with a left child but no right child. (Clearly, $\tilde{T}$ is a reverse Motzkin tree.) Let $\sigma$ be the result of appending $n$ to the beginning of $\alpha(\tilde{T})$ . It is easy to verify that the vertices of $T$ with exactly one child are precisely those vertices with labels belonging to $U\setminus\{\min U,\max U\}$ for some $U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ . For each $U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)$ , form the branch $T_{U}\in\mathsf{Branch}(i_{U})$ on the vertex set $U\setminus\{\max U\}$ by placing the elements of $U\setminus\{\max U\}$ in decreasing order from top to bottom. For each $k\in U\setminus\{\min U,\max U\}$ , the vertex $k\in T_{U}$ has a left (respectively, right) child if and only if the vertex labeled $k$ in $T$ has a left (respectively, right) child. Let $\Phi^{-1}(T)=(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})$ .

The functions $\Phi$ and $\Phi^{-1}$ described above are inverses. Therefore, $\Phi$ is a bijection. It follows directly from the definition of $\Phi^{-1}$ that if $\Phi(\sigma,(T_{U})_{U\in\mathrm{druns}(\sigma)})=T$ , then the multiset of branches $T_{U}$ for $U\in\pi$ is $\mathsf{IF}(T)$ . This proves (8), so (i) is equivalent to (iii). This completes the proof. ∎

## 5. The Troupe Transform

Let $\mathbf{T}\subseteq\mathsf{BPT}(I)$ be a troupe. For $n\geq 1$ , define $\omega_{n}=|\mathbf{T}\cap\mathsf{Branch}_{n}|$ and $\widecheck{\omega}_{n}=|\mathbf{T}\cap\mathsf{BPT}_{n}|$ . The troupe transform, defined by Defant in 2022, is a function that transforms the sequence $(\omega_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ to the sequence $(\widecheck{\omega}_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ [Def22, Section 2.5]. In this section, we will show how to compute the troupe transform.

By Proposition 3.3, every sequence of nonnegative integers can arise as the sequence $(\omega_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ for some choice of the troupe $\mathbf{T}$ . Hence, to compute the troupe transform, it suffices to compute the sequence $(\widecheck{\omega}_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ from $(\omega_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ . In fact, we will do so in the generality of weighted troupes.

#### Theorem 5.1.

Let $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}\to\mathbb{K}$ be a weighted troupe. For $n\geq 1$ , let

$$ \omega_{n}=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T)\quad\text{and}\quad\widecheck{\omega}_{n}=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

Then, the generating functions

$$ \mathscr{B}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\omega_{n}t^{n}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathscr{T}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\widecheck{\omega}_{n}t^{n} $$

satisfy

$$ \mathscr{T}(t)=\mathscr{B}\left(\frac{t}{1-t\mathscr{T}(t)}\right). $$

#### Proof.

Let $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{K}[X]$ . We may then choose the functional $\varphi\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{K}$ in such a way that $\varphi(X)=0$ and, for all $n\geq 2$ , we have

$$ -B_{n}(X,\ldots,X)=\omega_{n-1} $$

in the noncommutative probability space $(\mathcal{A},\varphi)$ . By Theorem 4.1, we have

$$ -R_{n}(X,\ldots,X)=\widecheck{\omega}_{n-1} $$

for all $n\geq 2$ .

By [AHLV15, Equation 2.16], we have

$$ 1-B\left(\frac{t}{1+R(t)}\right)=\frac{1}{1+R(t)}, $$

where

$$ B(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}B_{n}(X,\ldots,X)t^{n} $$

is the ordinary generating function for the Boolean cumulants of $X$ and

$$ R(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}R_{n}(X,\ldots,X)t^{n} $$

is the ordinary generating function for the free cumulants of $X$ . It follows from (9) and (10) that $B(t)=-t\mathscr{B}(t)$ and $R(x)=-t\mathscr{T}(t)$ ; substituting into (11) yields the desired result. ∎

#### Corollary 5.2.

Let $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}\to\mathbb{K}$ be a weighted troupe. For $n\geq 1$ , let

$$ \omega_{n}=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T)\quad\text{and}\quad\widecheck{\omega}_{n}=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

Let

$$ \mathscr{B}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\omega_{n}t^{n}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathscr{T}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 1}\widecheck{\omega}_{n}t^{n}. $$

Then $\mathscr{B}(x)$ is algebraic over $\mathbb{K}[t]$ if and only if $\mathscr{T}(t)$ is.

#### Proof.

Suppose that $\mathscr{B}(t)$ is algebraic (over $\mathbb{K}[t]$ ). This means that there exists a nonzero bivariate polynomial $P$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{K}$ such that $P(t,\mathscr{B}(t))=0$ . By Theorem 5.1, we have

$$ P\left(\frac{t}{1-t\mathscr{T}(t)},\mathscr{T}(t)\right)=P\left(\frac{t}{1-t\mathscr{T}(t)},\mathscr{B}\left(\frac{t}{1-t\mathscr{T}(t)}\right)\right)=0. $$

By clearing the denominators in this equation, we find a nonzero bivariate polynomial $Q$ with coefficients in $\mathbb{K}$ such that $Q(t,\mathscr{T}(t))=0$ . Therefore, $\mathscr{T}(t)$ is algebraic.

Conversely, suppose that $\mathscr{T}(t)$ is algebraic. Then, so is the power series

$$ \mathscr{W}(t)=\frac{t}{1-t\mathscr{T}(t)}. $$

By Theorem 5.1, we have $\mathscr{T}(t)=\mathscr{B}(\mathscr{W}(t))$ , so $\mathscr{B}=\mathscr{T}\circ\mathscr{W}^{\langle-1\rangle}$ , where $\mathscr{W}^{\langle-1\rangle}$ denotes the compositional inverse of $\mathscr{W}$ . It is well known that the compositional inverse of an algebraic power series is algebraic and that the composition of two algebraic power series is algebraic. Therefore, $\mathscr{B}$ is algebraic. ∎

Theorems 5.1 and 5.2 answer [Def22, Question 9.1].

## 6. Applications to Permutation Enumeration

Fix $i_{1},\ldots,i_{n}\in I$ , and recall that there is a bijection $\alpha\colon\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})\to\mathfrak{S}_{n}$ that maps a decreasing binary plane tree $T$ to the permutation formed by reading the labels of the vertices of $T$ in inorder. Using this bijection, we can rewrite the sum from Theorem 4.1(i) as a sum over permutations rather than a sum over decreasing binary plane trees. This motivates us to understand the insertion factors of a decreasing binary plane tree $(T,\mathcal{L})\in\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ in terms of the permutation $\alpha(T,\mathcal{L})$ . We consider each insertion factor as a decreasing binary plane tree, where the labeling is just the restriction of $\mathcal{L}$ .

The plot of a word $w$ over the alphabet $\mathbb{Z}$ is the diagram that depicts the points $(i,w(i))$ for all $i\in[n]$ . It turns out that there is a simple way to read off the insertion factors of $\alpha^{-1}(w)$ from the plot of $w$ . A peak of $w$ is an index $p\in\{2,\ldots,n-1\}$ such that $w(p-1)<w(p)>w(p+1)$ . Let $p_{1}<\cdots<p_{\ell}$ be the peaks of $w$ . For $1\leq j\leq\ell$ , let $\mathrm{SE}_{j}(w)$ be the set of points in the plot of $w$ that lie weakly southeast of $(p_{j},w(p_{j}))$ but do not lie weakly southeast of any of the points $(p_{j^{\prime}},w(p_{j^{\prime}}))$ for $j<j^{\prime}\leq\ell$ . Let $\mathrm{SE}_{0}(w)$ be the set of points in the plot of $w$ that do not belong to $\bigcup_{j=1}^{\ell}\mathrm{SE}_{j}(w)$ . After normalizing, we can view each set $\mathrm{SE}_{j}(w)$ as the plot of a word $w_{j}$ . Let $v_{j}$ be the vertex of $\alpha^{-1}(w)$ with label $w(p_{j})$ . Then $w_{j}$ is obtained by reading the labels of the insertion factor $T_{v_{j}}$ in inorder; this uniquely determines $T_{v_{j}}$ .

## 7. Cumulants from Distributions

Let us use the setup of Theorem 4.1. Suppose that $I=\{\star\}$ is a singleton, that $\mathbb{K}=\mathbb{R}$ , and that $\mathcal{A}=\mathbb{R}[X]$ , where $X=X_{\star}$ . Further, for any rapidly decreasing (Schwartz) distribution $f$ on $\mathbb{R}$ with total mass $1$ , define the linear functional $\varphi_{f}\colon\mathcal{A}\to\mathbb{R}$ by

$$ \varphi_{f}(X^{n})=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^{n}f(x)\,dx $$

for all $n\geq 0$ . Then $(\mathcal{A},\varphi_{f})$ is a commutative probability space. If $f$ is a probability distribution (i.e., it is nonnegative), then $(\mathcal{A},\varphi_{f})$ is genuinely a space of random variables.

When we refer to the $n$ th classical cumulant of a distribution $f$ , we mean the classical cumulant $K_{n}(X,\ldots,X)$ computed in the probability space $(\mathcal{A},\varphi_{f})$ . We use the notation $\kappa_{n}(f)$ for this quantity. Similarly, we define the $n$ th free and Boolean cumulants of the distribution $f$ , denoted $r_{n}(f)$ and $b_{n}(f)$ , respectively.

Classical cumulants satisfy the fundamental property that for all rapidly decreasing distributions $f,g$ , we have

$$ \kappa_{n}(f\ast g)=\kappa_{n}(f)+\kappa_{n}(g), $$

where $\ast$ denotes convolution.

We will consider some particular examples of weighted troupes $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}\to\mathbb{R}$ . For each such example, we attempt to exhibit a distribution $f$ such that the three conditions of Theorem 4.1 actually hold in the probability space $(\mathcal{A},\varphi_{f})$ . In other words, we want the following three equivalent conditions to hold for all $n\geq 1$ :

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{n}(f) \displaystyle=-\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}}\bm{\tau}(T), \displaystyle r_{n}(f) \displaystyle=-\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n-1}}\bm{\tau}(T), \displaystyle b_{n}(f) \displaystyle=-\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n-1}}\bm{\tau}(T). $$

(We remind the reader that if $I=\{\star\}$ is a singleton, then the set $\mathsf{DBPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})$ appearing in the statement of Theorem 4.1 is $\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}$ , not $\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}$ . Similarly, $\mathsf{BPT}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})=\mathsf{BPT}_{n-1}$ and $\mathsf{Branch}(i_{1},\ldots,i_{n})=\mathsf{Branch}_{n-1}$ .) The distribution $f$ will not necessarily be a probability distribution.

### 7.1. Binary Plane Trees

Suppose that $\bm{\tau}$ is the indicator function of $\mathsf{BPT}\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ . Then, for all $n\geq 1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=|\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}|=n!, \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=|\mathsf{BPT}_{n}|=C_{n}, \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=|\mathsf{Branch}_{n}|=2^{n-1}. $$

Hence, the condition (13) becomes

$$ \kappa_{n}(f)=\begin{cases}-(n-1)!&\mbox{if $n>1$}\\
0&\mbox{if $n=1$}\end{cases} $$

for all $n\geq 1$ . This is impossible if $f$ is a probability distribution. Indeed, if $f$ is a probability distribution, then $\kappa_{2}(f)$ is its variance, which is nonnegative and thus cannot be equal to $-1$ . However, it is possible to construct a distribution $f$ satisfying (13), as follows.

Let

$$ g(x)=\begin{cases}e^{-x+1}&\mbox{if $x\geq-1$}\\
0&\mbox{otherwise.}\end{cases} $$

This is the standard exponential distribution shifted so that its mean is $0$ . It is well known that the $n$ th classical cumulant of the standard exponential distribution is $(n-1)!$ [RS00], so

$$ \kappa_{n}(g)=\begin{cases}(n-1)!&\mbox{if $n>1$}\\
0&\mbox{if $n=1$.}\end{cases} $$

Now, let

$$ f(x)=\delta(x-1)+\delta^{\prime}(x-1), $$

where $\delta$ denotes the Dirac delta distribution. It is not difficult to check that $f$ is the convolution inverse of $g$ ; i.e. $f\ast g=\delta$ . By (12), we have $\kappa_{n}(f)=-\kappa_{n}(g)$ for all $n\geq 1$ , so $f$ indeed satisfies (13). By Theorem 4.1, $f$ satisfies (14) and (15) as well.

Note that for every integer $k\geq 0$ , the $k$ -fold convolution $g^{\ast k}$ is the well known gamma distribution with shape parameter $k$ , shifted to have mean $0$ . Thus, we may informally think of $f$ as the “gamma distribution with shape parameter $-1$ ”, shifted to have mean $0$ .

### 7.2. Binary Plane Trees Weighted by Right Edges

Fix a real number $q$ . Consider the weighted troupe $\bm{\tau}\colon\mathsf{BPT}\to\mathbb{R}$ defined by $\bm{\tau}(T)=q^{\mathrm{right}(T)+1}$ for all nonempty $T$ , where $\mathrm{right}(T)$ is the number of right edges in $T$ . If $q=1$ , then this coincides with the weighted troupe considered in Section 7.1; hence, we will assume in what follows that $q\neq 1$ . For all $n\geq 1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=qA_{n}(q), \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=qN_{n}(q), \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=q(1+q)^{n-1}, $$

where $A_{n}(t)$ and $N_{n}(t)$ denote the $n$ th Eulerian polynomial and the $n$ th Narayana polynomial, respectively [Def22, Example 6.3].

Let

$$ f(x)=\frac{\delta(x-q)-q\delta(x-1)}{1-q}. $$

We can check that $f$ satisfies (13) directly as follows. The moment-generating function of $f$ is

$$ M_{X}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\varphi_{f}(X^{n})\frac{t^{n}}{n!}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{tx}f(x)\,dx=\frac{e^{qt}-qe^{t}}{1-q}. $$

Therefore, by (4), we have

$$ \sum_{n\geq 0}\kappa_{n}(f)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}=\log\left(\frac{e^{qt}-qe^{t}}{1-q}\right). $$

From this, it is straightforward to check that

$$ \kappa_{n}(f)=\begin{cases}-qA_{n-1}(q)&\mbox{if $n>1$}\\
0&\mbox{if $n=1$,}\end{cases} $$

so $f$ satisfies (13), as desired. By Theorem 4.1, $f$ satisfies (14) and (15) as well.

Suppose that $|q|<1$ . Motivated by Section 7.1, we find that the convolution inverse of $f$ is

$$ g(x)=(1-q)\sum_{m\geq 0}q^{m}\delta(x+q-(1-q)m). $$

The distribution $g$ satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\kappa_{n}(g)=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}}\tau(T)=\begin{cases}-qA_{n-1}(q)&\mbox{if $n>1$}\\
0&\mbox{if $n=1$}.\end{cases} $$

If $0\leq q<1$ , then $g$ is a shifted and rescaled geometric distribution with success probability $1-q$ .

### 7.3. Full Binary Plane Trees

In each of the previous two examples (Sections 7.1 and 7.2), we found two distributions $f$ and $g$ which were convolution inverses of each other. The distribution $f$ was chosen to satisfy (13); that is,

$$ \kappa_{n}(f)=-\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}}\bm{\tau}(T) $$

for all $n\geq 1$ . (By Theorem 4.1, $f$ satisfied (14) and (15) as well.) On the other hand, the distribution $g$ satisfied the equation

$$ \kappa_{n}(g)=\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n-1}}\bm{\tau}(T) $$

for all $n\geq 1$ , which differs only in that it has no negative sign.

Recall that a nonempty binary plane tree is full if no vertex has exactly one child. Let $\mathsf{FBPT}$ be the troupe of full binary plane trees. Let $\bm{\tau}$ denote the indicator function of $\mathsf{FBPT}$ . For all $n\geq 1$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{DBPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}a_{n}&\mbox{if $n$ is odd}\\
0&\mbox{if $n$ is even},\end{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{BPT}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}C_{(n-1)/2}&\mbox{if $n$ is odd}\\
0&\mbox{if $n$ is even},\end{cases} \displaystyle\sum_{T\in\mathsf{Branch}_{n}}\bm{\tau}(T) \displaystyle=\begin{cases}1&\mbox{if $n=1$}\\
0&\mbox{otherwise},\end{cases} $$

where $a_{n}$ is the number of alternating permutations of size $n$ [Def22, Example 4.8]; the numbers $a_{1},a_{3},a_{5},\ldots$ are also known as tangent numbers since they are the coefficients of the Taylor series for the tangent function.

Let $\bm{\tau}$ be the indicator function of $\mathsf{FBPT}$ . We will still be able to exhibit a distribution $g$ satisfying (16). However, in contrast to Sections 7.1 and 7.2, the distribution $g$ does not have a convolution inverse, so there is no distribution $f$ satisfying (13) (and by Theorem 4.1, there is no distribution $f$ satisfying (14) or (15) either).

Let

$$ g(x)=\frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)+\exp\left(-\frac{\pi x}{2}\right)}; $$

then $g$ is the hyperbolic secant distribution. It is well known [Fis14, Section 1.3] that the moment-generating function of $g$ is

$$ M_{X}(t)=\sum_{n\geq 0}\varphi_{g}(X^{n})\frac{t^{n}}{n!}=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{tx}g(x)\,dx=\sec t, $$

so by (4), we have

$$ \sum_{n\geq 0}\kappa_{n}(g)\frac{t^{n}}{n!}=\log(\sec t). $$

Differentiating with respect to $t$ , we have

$$ \sum_{n\geq 1}\kappa_{n}(g)\frac{t^{n-1}}{(n-1)!}=\frac{d}{dt}\log(\sec t)=\tan t, $$

so $\kappa_{n}(g)$ is the coefficient of $t^{n-1}/(n-1)!$ in the Taylor series for $\tan t$ . That is,

$$ \kappa_{n}(g)=\begin{cases}a_{n}&\mbox{if $n$ is odd}\\
0&\mbox{if $n$ is even},\end{cases} $$

so $g$ satisfies (16) as desired.

It is unclear whether the hyperbolic secant distribution $g$ has any combinatorial meaning related to the troupe $\mathsf{FBPT}$ .
